case.case_title: Joseph Perera Alias Bruten Perera v. The Attorney-General and Others

clause.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether Regulation 28 of the Emergency Regulations violates the equality before the law guaranteed by Article 12(1) of the Constitution by permitting arbitrary and capricious exercise of power.
case_context.petitioner_claim: Regulation 28 is ultra vires and violates Article 12(1) because it confers unguided and arbitrary discretion on police officers to grant or refuse permission to distribute posters, handbills or leaflets, thus violating equality before the law.
case_context.respondent_argument: The respondents argued that the petitioners violated Regulation 28 by distributing posters and leaflets without police permission, justifying their arrest and detention.
key_facts: Petitioners distributed posters and leaflets without police permission as required by Regulation 28.
Regulation 28 requires prior police permission for distribution of any posters, handbills or leaflets.
Regulation 28 confers absolute and uncontrolled discretion on police officers without guiding principles.
Petitioners were arrested and detained based on alleged violation of Regulation 28.
The police did not have objective standards to guide their discretion under Regulation 28.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The court held that Article 12(1) guarantees equality before the law and prohibits arbitrary and discriminatory state action. Regulation 28 violates this principle by granting police officers unguided and absolute discretion to permit or refuse distribution of materials, lacking any objective standards or reasons for refusal. Such arbitrary power is the antithesis of equality before the law.
reasoning.application_to_facts: Since Regulation 28 allows police to arbitrarily grant or refuse permission without any guiding principles, it violates the constitutional guarantee of equality before the law. The petitioners' arrest and detention based on this regulation is therefore invalid.
principles_established: Equality before the law prohibits arbitrary and capricious exercise of state power.
Regulations conferring unguided discretion on officials violate Article 12(1).
Prior restraint requiring police permission must have narrow, objective, and definite standards.
Absence of such standards renders the regulation unconstitutional.

outcome.holding: Regulation 28 violates Article 12(1) of the Constitution and is invalid. The petitioners' arrest and detention based on this regulation cannot be justified.
outcome.remedy_or_orders: Regulation 28 declared invalid; petitioners entitled to relief for violation of fundamental rights.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 12(1) is central to the court's reasoning that the arbitrary discretion granted by Regulation 28 violates equality before the law, leading to the invalidation of the regulation and relief for the petitioners.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: Regulation 28 confers a naked and arbitrary power on the Police to grant or refuse permission to distribute pamphlets or posters as it pleases, in exercise of its absolute and uncontrolled discretion, without any guiding principle or policy to control and regulate the exercise of such discretion. This violates the constitutional mandate of equality before the law and is void.
